ground_truth.description: The class's stated contract was that the MCP tool 'get_scheduler_state' serves a 1500-task snapshot under 50ms, but the test now times only the sync helper 'read_scheduler_state', bypassing the asyncio.to_thread handoff and FastMCP dispatch entirely. A regression in the actual MCP request path that blows the 50ms orchestrator budget would no longer be caught by this canary, so perf coverage of the promised end-to-end path is lost.

The change removes asyncio/FastMCP overhead but keeps an absolute wall-clock 50ms bound measured with time.perf_counter, which still includes OS scheduling latency. Under pytest-xdist -n auto with 32 workers on a contended CPU, the process can be descheduled for tens of milliseconds during json.loads of the ~500KB file, so the median-of-20 assertion can still intermittently trip — the de-flake root cause (CI load sensitivity of a wall-clock latency bound) is only partially addressed.

The non-trivial-read guard checks only len(result['skip_counts']) == n; asserting result == snapshot once after the timing loop would check the whole payload at no cost to the timed region and make the ten-line justification comment unnecessary. Minor, since json.loads is all-or-nothing and the length check already catches the empty-skeleton fallback.

Several factual claims in the new comments are false: the payload is called 'a ~500KB file' but json.dumps of the fixture is 114,675 bytes (~115KB); the docstring attributes flakiness to 'pytest-xdist -n auto with 32 workers' though pyproject sets only '-n auto' (worker count is machine-dependent); the warm-up comment says it absorbs 'OS page-cache warm-up' although _write_snapshot has just written the file; and the guard comment says 'json.loads of a non-existent path is microseconds' whereas read_bytes raises FileNotFoundError and json.loads never runs.

About 30-40 lines of new docstring and comments surround about 20 lines of test logic, and most of it is addressed to a reviewer rather than describing the code: rejected alternatives ('Do NOT loosen this to 150-250ms', 'Do NOT confuse this with an MCP-layer perf bound'), history ('vs. the previous 9-sample window'), task-id provenance (1230, 1335), and a ten-line block restating what the assertion message already says, naming the private _empty_skeleton().

The loop uses 'range(22)' and 'if i >= 2' to encode 2 warm-ups plus 20 measured samples; the two literals must be kept consistent by hand and a comment is needed to explain them. Named constants (or a separate warm-up loop) would remove the branch and the comment.

TestSnapshotPerformance now targets the sync helper fused_memory.mcp_tools.scheduler_state.read_scheduler_state directly, but still sits in test_scheduler_state_tools.py whose other classes exercise the MCP tool surface via create_mcp_server, and its class name does not say it tests the helper rather than the tool.

task.title: test_scheduler_state_tools: de-flake 50ms perf assertion
task.description: The 50ms median latency test with 9 samples is flake-prone on loaded CI. Mark @perf or measure helper directly.
task.details:
From post-merge review of task 1230 (reviewer_comprehensive).

**Location:** `fused-memory/tests/test_scheduler_state_tools.py:343-362` (`TestSnapshotPerformance`)

**Issue:** The 50 ms median latency test is timing-sensitive and prone to flake under loaded CI (file is hundreds of KB; JSON parse + `asyncio.to_thread` roundtrip can easily exceed 50 ms on a busy runner). 9 samples after a one-sample warm-up is too small for a tail-sensitive assertion. A flake here will block unrelated PRs.

**Suggested fix:** One of:
(a) Loosen threshold (150-250 ms) with a comment noting it's a regression canary.
(b) Mark with `@pytest.mark.perf` and exclude from default CI.
(c) Measure only the synchronous helper (`read_scheduler_state`) directly to remove asyncio/MCP overhead from the budget.

**Acceptance:**
- Either threshold raised + comment, or `@pytest.mark.perf` excluded from default CI, or test rewritten against the sync helper.
- No flake under 5 consecutive CI runs on a typical loaded runner.
